parsed.explanation: Two competing frameworks both criminalise same-sex intimacy (six months to three years under the administering state, up to three years under the movement's listing), and a trans visitor whose relationship is read against birth sex stands inside that prohibition. No source records any trans-specific protection, anti-discrimination mechanism, or hate-crime recourse anywhere in the territory, and the administering state's courts and detention demonstrably operate over the ground, including on political cases. Social reading of same-sex relationships as foreign is documented. Against this, no trans-specific statute, no documented processing of a trans visitor, no border-exclusion regime, no organised targeting and no lethal custody are recorded; the prison exposure is conditional on discovery and on a relationship being read as same-sex. Thin-data extrapolation from standing criminalisation plus absent recourse places this near the 0.25 tier, not the 0.35 exclusion/administrative tier.

entry_documents.exposure: Not documented. No border, marker or document rule for trans visitors is recorded under either framework.
entry_documents.interaction: Which framework governs depends on which part of the territory is entered; both criminalise same-sex conduct, so entry does not change legality, only administration.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Standing imprisonment penalty (six months to three years; up to three years under the movement's listing) for same-sex intimacy, which can attach to a trans visitor read against birth sex. Camp officials documented holding prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges without a court.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: None documented; the exile constitution's silence is not decriminalisation.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Administering-state courts and detention operate on the territory (2005 defenders' trial); camp charges sit with administration rather than courts.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Not documented. No facility-access, ward-placement or custody-placement rule for trans people is recorded.

care_services.exposure: Not documented. No trans-specific care, medication or refusal evidence in the inventory.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Criminal prohibition of same-sex conduct under both frameworks; social reading of such relationships as a foreign phenomenon; no legal protection against discrimination or violence per a refugee-aid organisation.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: None documented; the 2010 diplomatic statement is a position, not a legal text.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Enforcement machinery is real: the administering state's courts and detention handle territory cases, so a hostile rule would be enforced rather than dormant.

minors_guardians.exposure: Not documented. No evidence on trans minors or guardians travelling in the territory.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No trans-specific violence recorded. No protection mechanism exists for LGBTQ people facing discrimination or violence, so recourse is effectively absent.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Absence of recourse means any hostility would go unmediated by protective institutions.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No remedy, ombudsman, complaint body or anti-discrimination route documented under either framework.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Whether either authority would apply a same-sex provision to a trans person, and on what reading of legal sex, is entirely unsourced.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar tier: standing criminal exposure and absent protection, without the documented raids, fines and extortion that anchor specifies. Here the potential penalty is heavier (imprisonment up to three years) but no trans-targeted enforcement pattern is recorded, keeping it close to this level rather than above it.

Lower: that anchor has a routine, visitor-specific border-exclusion regime reaching every visibly trans traveller. This dossier records no visitor-facing entry screening against trans people, only a conduct statute, so the exposure is conditional rather than universal at the border.

Considerably lower: that anchor has documented secondary screening, refused admission and humiliating searches of trans visitors with an appeal desk. Here nothing documents a trans visitor being processed at all; the documented harm is criminalisation of conduct plus absent recourse, a heavier but less evidenced exposure.

Far lower: that anchor documents functioning tribunals, enforceable remedies and compensation. This territory documents no protective mechanism of any kind, only criminal prohibition and unmediated camp administration.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime is criminalisation without recourse. Same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment under both competing frameworks, so moving between administered and movement-controlled areas changes the administrator, not the legality. The administering state's courts and detention demonstrably reach the territory, meaning a hostile provision would be enforced rather than left dormant; camp officials are recorded detaining people on 'homosexuality' charges outside court process. Social stigma is documented. Mitigating: nothing trans-specific is recorded — no border screening, no facility exclusion, no organised targeting, no lethal custody, no documented processing of a trans visitor — and the prison exposure requires discovery plus a relationship read against birth sex. Thin-data extrapolation from standing criminalisation, absent protection and functioning enforcement places the rating in the high-risk band, near but above the 0.25 tier.
